## Abstract

A comprehensive assessment of genetic modulators of KRAS inhibitor sensitivity identifies combination approaches to increase the efficacy of KRAS inhibitors and demonstrates the limited response of KRASQ61H-mutant cancer cells to KRAS inhibition.

## Abstract

KRAS inhibitors (KRASi) targeting various KRAS mutations have entered clinical trials for pancreatic cancer. Despite promising preliminary clinical responses, most patients relapse due to intrinsic or acquired resistance. Thus, combination treatments are essential to extend the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapies. To further determine the genetic mechanisms of KRASi resistance, we performed KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function screens in KRASG12D-, KRASG12C-, KRASG12R-, and KRASQ61H-mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cell lines, using six KRASi, to identify genes that modulate sensitivity to KRAS inhibition. Several hits from the screens, including EGFR, CK2, p110α, p110γ, and YAP, were validated by combining targeted inhibitors with KRASi. KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines were intrinsically less dependent on KRAS for survival than other KRAS mutational subtypes. Furthermore, the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib synergized with the RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor RMC-7977 in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines and in cell lines with highly active EGFR by mitigating ERK rebound activity. KRASi-resistant cell lines featured sustained ERK/MAPK dependence despite decreased ERK activity. Together, these findings enhance the understanding of intrinsic and acquired resistance to KRASi and identify therapeutic vulnerabilities that can potentially be exploited for KRASi combination therapies in patients with pancreatic cancer.

A comprehensive assessment of genetic modulators of KRAS inhibitor sensitivity identifies combination approaches to increase the efficacy of KRAS inhibitors and demonstrates the limited response of KRASQ61H-mutant cancer cells to KRAS inhibition.

## Introduction

Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest cancers, with a 5-year survival rate of only 13% (1). Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common and lethal pancreatic cancer subtype, is associated with an 8% 5-year survival rate and a 94% KRAS mutation frequency (1–3). KRAS is a small GTPase that cycles between an active GTP-bound ON state and an inactive GDP-bound OFF state (3). Activating mutations in KRAS lead to persistent GTP loading and hyperactivation, serving as an initiating event in the transformation of the normal pancreatic epithelium and a requirement for tumor maintenance (4–7). The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to two mutant-specific KRASG12C inhibitors for non–small cell lung cancer (8, 9). Two limitations remain before KRAS therapeutic inhibitors can be widely deployed for patients with PDAC. First, only 1% of patients with KRAS-mutant PDAC have KRASG12C mutations, leaving the remaining 99% without a clinically approved KRASi therapeutic option (3). Second, KRAS inhibitors (KRASi) are limited by intrinsic and acquired resistance (10–15).

To address the first issue, we recently described RMC-7977, a RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor that targets the GTP-bound “ON” state of a broad range of KRAS-, NRAS-, and HRAS-mutant variants, as well as the wild-type (WT) isoforms (16, 17). Daraxonrasib (RMC-6236), the clinical analog, is undergoing phase III trials in patients with PDAC (NCT06625320) and has received orphan drug and Breakthrough Therapy designation from the FDA (18, 19). Although preliminary clinical responses with daraxonrasib are impressive (19), combination therapies will be necessary to improve the depth and durability of the response for most patients (20).

Our current understanding of resistance mechanisms to KRASi in PDAC is limited for several reasons. First, most putative resistance mechanisms identified in KRASG12C inhibitor-treated patients involve evaluating patient blood for circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) using limited mutation panels targeting a subset of genes. Second, the frequency of KRASG12C mutations is low (1%). Third, in roughly half of patients, no known genetic resistance drivers can be identified after tumor progression (2). Fourth, cell state changes, like epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions (EMT) without known genetic mechanisms, are also purported to drive resistance to KRASi (10, 11, 13, 21–23). To address this gap in knowledge, we performed 12 KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 loss-of-function (LOF) screens with six different KRASi in six PDAC cell lines with various KRAS mutations.

From our screens, we identified many KRASi resistance mechanisms that have been observed in relapsed patients and discovered additional novel therapeutic vulnerabilities. In this study, we found that the EGFR inhibitor (EGFRi) erlotinib synergized with the RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor RMC-7977 in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC, which is less responsive to KRASi, by mitigating ERK activity rebound. We further validated emerging therapeutic targets CK2 and p110γ as modulators of KRASi resistance. Finally, we generated a panel of RMC-7977-resistant PDAC cell lines and evaluated inhibitor sensitivity and cross-resistance in our resistant lines. Our results suggest there will be many shared resistance mechanisms, as well as heterogeneous resistance mechanisms that vary by inhibitor mechanism of action (MOA) and KRAS mutational subtype.

## Materials and Methods

### Cell culture

Pa01C, Pa02C, Pa04C, Pa14C, and Pa16C cell lines were obtained from A. Maitra (MD Anderson Cancer Center; ref. 24). The remaining PDAC cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Cell lines were routinely tested for Mycoplasma using the MycoAlert kit (Lonza) and always tested negative. Cells were maintained in DMEM or RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS. Short tandem repeat profiling was performed on all cell lines before screening. PDM-36 PDAC organoids were purchased from the ATCC. Organoids were seeded in Cultrex basement membrane extract (BME) and maintained in advanced DMEM/F12 supplemented with 1× B27 supplement, 10 mmol/L HEPES, 1× GlutaMAX, 1× penicillin/streptomycin (10,000 U/mL), 0.2 nmol/L recombinant WNT surrogate–Fc fusion, 10 mmol/L nicotinamide, 1.25 mmol/L N-acetyl-L-cysteine, 50 ng/mL recombinant hEGF, 100 ng/mL hFGF-10, 0.1 μg/mL recombinant hNoggin, 0.13 μg/mL recombinant hR-spondin 1, 10 nmol/L hGastrin I, and 500 nmol/L A83-01 (rhcomp medium). All cell line and organoid experiments were cultured at 37°C with 5% CO2 in humidity-controlled incubators. Cell lines, their RRIDs, and organoids utilized in this study are listed in Supplementary Table S1A.

### KRASi-anchored CRISPR LOF screens

The oncogenic pathway CRISPR-Cas9 library contains 2,388 pooled genes with five single-guide RNAs (sgRNA) per gene and an additional 50 control sgRNAs, as we previously reported (provided by K. Wood, Duke; refs. 25–27). Each cell line was transduced with lentiviral particles at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.2, starting with 3.2 × 108 cells per cell line, split among four 875 cm2 layered tissue culture flasks, followed by a media exchange after 24 hours. After an additional 24 hours, another media exchange was performed, including 2 μg/mL of puromycin to select for transduced cells. After selection, the puromycin concentration was halved, and cells were cultured for 7 days, allowing essential genes to be depleted. Cells were then split into 500 cm2 tissue culture plates at a concentration of 1.25 × 107 cells per plate and cultured independently throughout the screen. The next day, DMSO or the 50% growth inhibitory concentration (GI50) of KRASi was added to the plates.

Cells were grown for 4 to 5 weeks, exchanging KRASi every 3 to 4 days and passaging as necessary, maintaining 1.25 × 107 cells per plate (1,000× coverage of each sgRNA) in each technical replicate. We performed four technical replicates for most screens, cell line permitting. PSN-1 had two technical replicates. After 2 and 4 weeks of treatment, 1.25 × 107 cells were harvested for each DMSO- and KRASi-treated technical replicate. Genomic DNA was isolated from these samples using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (QIAGEN). The guide RNAs were PCR-amplified, followed by an additional PCR step to add indexing primers. The PCR product was run on a 2% agarose gel and purified by gel purification using the QIAquick gel extraction kit (QIAGEN). DNA concentrations for each sample were normalized with a Qubit Fluorometer (Invitrogen), and deep sequencing was performed on 3 pmol/L of DNA (10% PhiX spike) with an Illumina NextSeq 500/550 High Output 75 cycle kit on a NextSeq 500 DNA sequencer (Illumina). Enrichment/depletion of sgRNAs was assessed by MAGeCKFlute (28) analysis. Δβ Scores were calculated by subtracting the DMSO-treated β score from the KRASi-treated β score for each gene.

### Proliferation assays

Cell lines were passaged and seeded into the inner wells of 96-well plates at a density of 3 × 103 cells per well, and organoids were seeded at a density of 6 × 103 cells per well in 10% Cultrex BME in rhcomp medium, with a PBS ring in the outer wells to limit evaporation. The next day, plates were treated with the indicated compounds using a D300E Drug Dispenser (Tecan) and incubated for an additional 72 hours for cell lines and 120 hours for organoids. For traditional cell lines, proliferation was measured by incubating each well with 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) for 1 to 2 hours and then solubilizing the MTT with DMSO before reading absorbance at 570 nmol/L. For organoids, proliferation was measured using CellTiter-Glo, with a 1,000 ms integration time. Analyses were performed on a SpectraMax i3x multimode plate reader. XY graphs were analyzed with GraphPad Prism 10, and combination matrices were assessed with Combenefit using the highest single agent synergy model.

### Short hairpin RNA lentiviral transductions

We previously validated RAS isoform short hairpin RNAs (shRNA) for isoform selectivity (29). shRNAs targeting NRAS, HRAS, SOS1 (SOS1 Clone IDs TRCN0000065427 and TRCN0000048146), and LEF1 (LEF1 Clone IDs TRCN0000020162 and TRCN0000020163) were purchased as Escherichia coli glycerol stocks from Sigma-Aldrich. After purifying the shRNA-containing plasmid DNAs, 12 μg were mixed with 9 μg of psPAX2 and 3 μg of pMD2.G, before being diluted in 1 mL of Opti-MEM. FuGENE HD (72 μL) was added to the plasmid–Opti-MEM mixture and incubated for 8 to 10 minutes at room temperature before the transfection mixture was added to HEK293T cells, which had been plated the previous day at a concentration of 2 × 106 cells in a 75 cm2 tissue culture flask in 12 mL of DMEM + 10% FBS. The transfection mixture was replaced with DMEM + 10% FBS the next day and incubated for an additional 48 hours. Virus particles were filtered through a 0.45 μm filter, collected, and frozen at −80°C. PDAC cells (4 × 105) were plated in a 25 cm2 tissue culture flask and transduced the next day by combining 0.5 mL of virus with 8 μg/mL of polybrene in 3 mL of medium + 10% FBS, aspirating the spent culture medium, and replacing it with the virus/polybrene-containing medium. After 24 hours, the virus-containing medium was replaced with medium + 10% FBS. The following day, puromycin selection was performed over a course of 48 hours by replacing the culture medium with culture medium containing 2 μg/mL puromycin. After 48 hours, the puromycin concentration was halved, and cells were treated or assessed as described.

### Immunoblotting

Cells were washed with cold PBS and lysed with cold Triton X-100 buffer (20 mmol/L Tris HCl, 150 nmol/L NaCl, 1 mmol/L EDTA) containing protease (Sigma) and phosphatase inhibitors (Sigma) on ice. Cells were incubated for 5 minutes on ice before scraping the lysates into prechilled tubes. Cell lysates were centrifuged at >15,000 × g for 10 to 15 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected. Protein concentration normalization was performed with a bicinchoninic acid assay (Pierce), utilizing BSA as a standard. Equal protein amounts (10–20 μg depending on the experiment) were added to each gel, followed by standard immunoblotting procedures. Antibodies utilized in this study and their RRIDs are listed in Supplementary Table S1B. Nitrocellulose membranes were activated with methanol, and the membranes were blocked in 3% milk in TBS with Tween-20 for 1 hour. Wet transfers were performed at room temperature with an ice block in the gel box for 1 hour at 100 V.

### In vitro kinase assays

Recombinant human MYC (2.5 μg; Abcam) was incubated with 5,000 U of recombinant CK2 in 25 μL of 1× protein kinase buffer (New England Biolabs) containing 10 mmol/L ATP at 30°C for 30 minutes. To inhibit CK2 activity, 5 μmol/L silmitasertib was added to the reaction tube. Samples were heated to 95°C for 5 minutes and run on a 12% Mini-PROTEAN TGX gel (Bio-Rad) in 1× running buffer at 150 V for 45 minutes. Protein gels were stained with SimplyBlue SafeStain (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Core facilities utilized in this study and their RRIDs are listed in Supplementary Table S1C.

### In-gel digestion, LC/MS-MS analysis, and data processing

Protein bands corresponding to MYC were excised and destained, and the proteins were reduced, alkylated, and in-gel digested with trypsin overnight at 37°C as described (30). Peptides were extracted and dried by vacuum centrifugation. All peptide samples were stored at −80°C until further analysis.

LC/MS-MS analysis was performed on a Thermo Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer coupled to a Dionex UltiMate 3000 RSLCnano (Thermo Fisher Scientific), as described previously (31). Briefly, trypsin-digested peptides from the recombinant MYC/CK2 kinase reaction, with or without the CK2 inhibitor (CK2i) silmitasertib, were reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid and loaded onto a 5 mm nanoViper μ-Precolumn [internal diameter (i.d.) 300 mm, C18]. Peptides were separated on an EASY-Spray column PepMap RSLC C18 with a 150-mm column (i.d. 75 μm, C18, 3.0 μm, 100 Å; Thermo Fisher Scientific) over 30 minutes with a gradient of acetonitrile in 0.1% formic acid from 5% to 32% acetonitrile, at a flow rate of 300 nL/minute. MS1 data were collected over an m/z range of 375–2000 on the Orbitrap [60,000 resolution; automatic gain control (AGC), 4 × 105]. Charge states between 2 and 4 were required for MS2 analysis with a 20-second dynamic exclusion window and a cycle time of 2.5. MS2 scans were performed in an ion trap with higher-energy collisional dissociation fragmentation (isolation window, 0.8 Da; normalized collision energy, 30%; AGC, 5 × 104) and recorded using Xcalibur 4.3 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The raw files were searched using Proteome Discoverer version 3.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) against a human protein database and the Sequest HT search algorithm to identify peptides incorporating the IMP-ptmRS node to calculate probabilities of the phosphorylation sites. Extraction ion chromatograms (XIC) for indicated phosphopeptides were generated using FreeStyle 1.3 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). MS1 monoisotopic peptide masses at 5 ppm mass accuracy as XICs were compared based on the maximum intensity for the indicated phosphorylated peptides, with or without the addition of silmitasertib, and presented as a percentage of the maximal intensity.

### Autophagic flux assays

Cells stably expressing GFP-LC3-RFP-LC3ΔG were generated as described previously (32). GFP-LC3-RFP-LC3ΔG–expressing cells were plated and treated with indicated inhibitors 24 hours after plating. Following 24 or 72 hours of inhibitor treatment, cells were collected, washed, filtered to remove clumps, and resuspended in fresh media. Samples were analyzed using an Attune NxT from Thermo Fisher Scientific to quantify total GFP and red fluorescent protein (RFP) fluorescence. Data processing was performed using Attune Cytometric Software version 5.3.0. The autophagic index is displayed as a ratio of RFP/GFP.

### RNA sequencing

RNA was purified from AsPC-1, HPAC, HuP-T3, MIA PaCa-2, Pa01C, Pa04C, Pa14C, Pa16C, PANC-1, Pa02C, T3M4, and Hs766T cells at their second passage from liquid nitrogen thaw. After RNA isolation, 150 to 300 ng of RNA, determined by Qubit (Invitrogen) fluorimetry, was poly-A–selected and reverse-transcribed using Illumina’s TruSeq stranded mRNA library preparation kit. Each sample was fitted with one of 96 adaptors containing a different nine-base molecular barcode and PCR-amplified for 15 cycles. Completed libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000, generating greater than 50 million high-quality 100-base-long paired-end reads per sample. A quality control check on the FASTQ files was performed using FastQC. Upon passing basic quality metrics, the reads were trimmed to remove adapters and low-quality reads using default parameters in Trimmomatic version 0.33 (33). The trimmed reads were mapped to a reference genome using default parameters with the RF strandness option in HISAT2 version 2.0.5 (34). Transcript abundance was determined using Kallisto version 0.43.1 (35). We created a transcriptome index in Kallisto using Ensembl cDNA sequences for the reference genome. This index was then used to quantify transcript abundance in raw counts and transcripts per million (TPM). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed by Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center.

### Pathway analysis

We utilized bulk RNA-seq TPM values to classify human PDAC cell lines along the basal-like–classical spectrum using the Moffitt signatures (36) and the purity-independent subtyping [Purity Independent Subtyping of Tumors (PurIST); ref. 37] approach in an R environment (version 4.2.0). We utilized STRING-DB (38) to map the physical subnetwork of high-confidence interaction scores.

### Statistical analysis and rigor

All experiments are representative of between two and six biological replicates. Statistical details of experiments can be found in figure legends. Confidence intervals are denoted as follows: *, P < 0.05; **, P < 0.01; ***, P < 0.001; ****, P < 0.0001. All experiments were performed in at least biological triplicate unless otherwise noted. Online resources, databases, and software tools utilized in this study and their RRIDs are listed in Supplementary Table S1D and S1E.

## Results

### KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 LOF screens identify modulators of KRASi activity

Among the KRASi being evaluated, MOAs range from covalent to noncovalent and from “OFF” state switch II (SII) pocket inhibitors to ON-state inhibitors to OFF/ON inhibitors. Additionally, while some KRASi are mutant-selective, others are “pan”-KRAS or multiselective, targeting mutant and WT RAS molecules. Finally, degrader molecules that promote KRAS degradation are also being pursued (20). We and others have established that specific KRAS mutations cause distinct functional consequences (39–44), and different KRAS mutations exhibit distinct dependencies. To comprehensively assess genetic resistance mechanisms to KRASi with varying MOA, we performed 12 KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 LOF screens in two KRASG12D-, two KRASG12R-, one KRASQ61H-, and one KRASG12C-mutant PDAC cell line with GI50 of six different KRASi (Table 1; Fig. 1A). We performed the screens with three KRASG12C covalent inhibitors (8, 27, 45), one KRASG12D inhibitor (SII OFF/ON state; refs. 46, 47), and two RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitors (16). MRTX1257 is an analog of adagrasib, and RM-028 is an analog of RMC-7977 lacking the GTP hydrolysis properties (48).

We performed the screens over a period of 4 to 5 weeks and scored genes using MAGeCKFlute, based on their proliferative effect, in which negative Δβ scores indicate that the loss of that gene increases sensitivity to KRASi compared with DMSO (Supplementary Data Files S1–S7; ref. 28). Within the DMSO-treated samples, genes predicted to be essential in DepMap were also preferentially lost in our screen (Supplementary Fig. S1A and S1B).

We observed an initial depletion of cells after 1 week of KRASi treatment, which was eventually overtaken by clonal outgrowth by the end of the screen (Fig. 1B). First, we identified the most robust hits across the panel of KRAS-mutant cell lines using the Δβ scores from the terminal screening time point for each cell line. For cell lines in which only one KRASi was used, Δβ scores were rank-ordered. For cell lines in which multiple KRASi were used, Δβ scores were rank-ordered for each KRASi, and all KRASi rank-ordered scores for each gene were averaged together. Next, we averaged the rank-ordered gene-level scores for all cell lines together (Fig. 1C). We considered the top 10% of enriched and the top 10% of depleted genes as “hits” in the screen. Genes plotted in the bottom left indicate that the loss of these genes sensitizes cells to KRASi, whereas genes plotted in the top right indicate that the loss of these genes drives resistance to KRASi.

Our hits overlap with putative resistance mechanisms found to be mutated or amplified in relapsed patients treated with KRASG12C inhibitors (yellow). We also found several additional expected sensitizers [loss of MAPK1 (encodes ERK2), YAP1, and PTPN11 (encodes SHP2)] and resistance drivers (loss of NF2, LATS, FBXW7, and MST1). Loss of NF1 was differentially dysregulated (P = 0.009) between the two classes of KRASi, scoring as the 14th strongest sensitizing gene for SII inhibitors, but not scoring as a hit with RAS(ON) inhibitors. These results validate that our screens have the potential to identify both clinically relevant and novel resistance mechanisms. The top 10% of KRASi-sensitizing and resistance-driving genes are listed in Supplementary Fig. S1C and S1D.

We performed KEGG pathway analysis on the KRASi-sensitizing (Supplementary Table S2) and resistance-driving hits (Supplementary Table S3). Expectedly, ERBB, PI3K/Akt, and MAPK signaling pathways were highly enriched in KRASi sensitizing genes. Likewise, RAS, PI3K/Akt, and MAPK signaling pathways were highly enriched in KRASi resistance-driving genes. We then dissected differences between RAS(ON) multiselective hits and mutant-selective hits (Supplementary Tables S4 and S5). RMC-7977-selective sensitizing mechanisms involved pathways that were centered on metabolism and nucleotide biosynthesis and repair, whereas neurotrophin, MAPK, PI3K-Akt, and Hippo signaling pathways were more enriched in a mutant-selective KRASi context.

At the conclusion of the screen, we lysed an aliquot of surviving cells to evaluate signaling dynamics. We determined that the resistant cells remaining at the end of the screens had elevated EGFR, ERK, and Akt activity, as well as increased MYC expression (Fig. 1D). Taken together, these data indicate that putative resistance mechanisms found in patients are recapitulated in our screens, and the EGFR–RAS–ERK MAPK/PI3K–MYC axis may be critical in driving resistance to KRASi in PDAC.

### Validating screening hits utilizing orthogonal pharmacologic approaches

When determining which hits, we prioritized validating translationally relevant hits for which pharmacologic inhibitors already existed. Loss of EGFR was a strong sensitizing gene to KRASi, EGFR activity was upregulated in the cells that persisted upon long-term KRASi treatment, EGFR amplification has been identified as a putative resistance mechanism to KRASi in patients with PDAC (10), and erlotinib is an FDA-approved EGFRi for PDAC.

We began by combining erlotinib with mutant-selective KRASi MRTX1133 and adagrasib and performing proliferation assays (Supplementary Fig. S2A and S2B). We confirmed, as expected, that erlotinib and MRTX1133/adagrasib synergize to reduce growth in all three cell lines assessed. These data mimic what was recently published (49). One well-accepted model describes how synergy occurs between SII KRASi and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitors. Upon KRASi treatment, negative feedback mechanisms lead to increased RTK activity and increased activation of WT RAS molecules that result in the reactivation of ERK to drive growth (50).

Our screening data indicated that the loss of YAP1 was a strong sensitizer to KRASi and that the loss of NF2, MST1, and LATS2, upstream tumor suppressors in the Hippo pathway, drove resistance. We and others have recently determined that IAG933, a YAP/TAZ-TEAD complex inhibitor, synergizes with KRASG12C inhibitors to reduce growth in KRASG12C-mutant PDAC by multiple mechanisms (27, 51). In the absence of KRAS signaling, YAP-TEAD signaling compensates through TEAD-driven activation of PI3K signaling, expression of ERK transcriptional targets, and in vivo by promoting MYC activity (17). Thus, to determine if we could extend these data in vitro, we treated PDAC cell lines with the combination of RMC-7977 and the YAP/TAZ-TEAD inhibitor IAG933 (Supplementary Fig. S2C). IAG933 synergized with RMC-7977 in all nine KRAS-mutant PDAC lines we evaluated. Validation of EGFR and YAP provides further confirmation that our screens can be useful for identifying KRASi resistance mechanisms that may arise in patients.

### Erlotinib synergizes with RMC-7977 in a subset of PDAC cell lines

We previously demonstrated that RMC-7977 inhibited both mutant KRAS and all WT RAS isoforms (16). Based on the established mechanism (50), we anticipated that we would not see synergy when we combined RMC-7977 with an EGFRi. Thus, we were surprised that the loss of EGFR scored as a hit in RMC-7977–specific screens. To validate this pharmacologically, we treated a panel of 12 KRAS-mutant PDAC cell lines with the combination of RMC-7977 and erlotinib (Fig. 2A). We observed synergistic growth suppression in a subset of PDAC cell lines. The synergistic cell lines also exhibited a more pronounced growth defect from single-agent erlotinib treatment (Supplementary Fig. S2D). We observed strong synergy in two of the three KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC lines and three of the nine KRASG12X-mutant PDAC cell lines.

We considered that some cell lines may be reliant on the alternative ERBB family proteins HER2 or HER4. Thus, utilizing four cell lines in which we did not observe synergistic growth suppression with RMC-7977 and erlotinib, we combined RMC-7977 with the pan-ERBB inhibitor afatinib. In three of four cell lines, there were modest increases in synergistic growth suppression, indicating that some KRASG12X cell lines may be broadly dependent on ERBB signaling (Supplementary Fig. S2E).

### KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines are pharmacologically and genetically less dependent on KRAS for survival

We recently determined that KRASQ61H-mutant cell lines were more insensitive to KRAS inhibition with RMC-7977 (16). It was also recently reported that RMC-7977 induces GTP hydrolysis when the inhibitory tricomplex is formed, but more weakly in KRASQ61H-mutant cells, suggesting a proposed mechanism for the decreased RMC-7977 sensitivity (48). Consistently, we also determined that KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines exhibited a smaller decrease in active ERK than KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cell lines after RMC-7977 treatment (Fig. 2B).

To determine if our findings of impaired potency in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC were limited to RMC-7977, we assessed the potency of BI-2865 and AMG 410, two SII pan-KRASi, in a panel of KRASQ61H- and KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cell lines. Similar to RMC-7977, we determined that BI-2865 and AMG 410 were less potent in KRASQ61H-mutant lines (Fig. 2C and D), indicating that there are additional mechanisms besides reduced GTP hydrolysis with RMC-7977 that underlie the decreased KRAS sensitivity in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC.

Notably, we also recently discovered that KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines were genetically less dependent on KRAS for survival than other mutational subtypes (2). We also found that the decreased KRAS genetic dependence in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines extends across cancer types (Supplementary Fig. S2F). From our orthogonal findings that KRASQ61H-mutant cells are both genetically and pharmacologically less dependent on KRAS for survival, we conclude that the decreased sensitivity can be primarily attributed to KRASQ61H mutation biology rather than a specific KRASi. We further determined that KRASQ61H has a poor prognosis compared with other KRAS mutational subtypes (Supplementary Fig. S2G), indicating that uncovering the underlying mechanisms behind this has translational relevance.

### WT RAS reactivates ERK in an SOS1-dependent manner after KRASi treatment in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines

To determine whether the higher levels of active ERK in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC were due to weaker pathway inhibition or active ERK rebound, we evaluated the ability of RMC-7977 to reduce ERK activity in these lines temporally (Fig. 3A). We observed a near-complete loss of active ERK at 2 hours that began rebounding rapidly after 4 hours of treatment, indicating that initially, RMC-7977 is potent in KRASQ61H-mutant models, followed by a rapid active ERK rebound. Notably, this active ERK rebound was more rapid than in KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S2H; ref. 16).

To evaluate whether the increased active ERK rebound was due to increases in WT RAS activity, we assessed the level of GTP-bound RAS after acute RMC-7977 treatment in KRASQ61H- and KRASG12D-mutant cell lines, using RAS isoform-selective antibodies (Fig. 3B; ref. 29). We observed increased HRAS and NRAS activity in KRASQ61H-mutant cell lines, but not in KRASG12D-mutant cell lines. We and others had previously determined that KRASQ61H is biochemically distinct from other KRAS mutational subtypes in two major ways (39, 42, 43, 52, 53). First, the SOS1–RASQ61H interaction is defective, and second, RASQ61H binds tightly (albeit nonfunctionally) to GAPs such as NF1, acting as an NF1 inhibitor (42, 43). Thus, we hypothesized that KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cells may be especially reliant on RTK signaling for WT RAS activation and that upon RMC-7977 treatment, SOS1 can rapidly activate WT RAS. To evaluate this, we assessed whether SOS1 genetic suppression impaired compensatory WT RAS GTP loading after RMC-7977 treatment in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines (Fig. 3C). In support of our hypothesis, we observed a striking increase in HRAS-GTP and NRAS-GTP levels after 72 hours of RMC-7977 treatment that was abrogated upon SOS1 knockdown (T3M4 cells are heterozygous for KRASQ61H, and Pa02C cells are homozygous for KRASQ61H).

We next genetically suppressed SOS1, HRAS, NRAS, or the combination of HRAS and NRAS to evaluate whether KRASQ61H-mutant cells are dependent on these proteins for survival (Fig. 3D and E). We determined that genetic suppression of any component reduced growth in KRASQ61H-mutant T3M4 and Pa02C cells, indicating they are partially dependent on these proteins for survival. Additionally, genetic suppression of any of these components also further sensitized KRASQ61H-mutant T3M4 cells to RMC-7977 (Fig. 3F). In contrast, genetic suppression of SOS1 did not sensitize KRASG12D-mutant cell lines to RMC-7977 (Fig. 3G; Supplementary Fig. S3A and S3B). Thus, SOS1 rapidly increases GTP loading of WT RAS isoforms to reactivate ERK in RMC-7977-treated KRASQ61H-, but not KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cells. Therefore, we conclude that KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines are more resistant to KRASi because they are more dependent on SOS1 and WT HRAS and NRAS, likely due to the established biochemical idiosyncrasies (Fig. 4A; refs. 39, 42, 43, 52, 53).

### Combining RMC-7977 and erlotinib causes synergistic proliferative defects in a subset of PDAC cell lines

When evaluating the KRASQ61H-mutant T3M4 CRISPR screening data in isolation, loss of EGFR, PTPN11, and MAPK1 was the fourth, eighth, and twelfth strongest respective sensitizers in the screen, whereas loss of NF1 drove resistance (Supplementary Fig. S3C). Further, when we combined erlotinib with RMC-7977 treatment for 72 hours, all four combinations tested mitigated the RMC-7977–induced active ERK rebound, suggesting that reduced ERK rebound mechanistically contributes to the observed synergy (Fig. 4B).

Conversely, when combining erlotinib with RMC-7977 in Pa14C cells, a KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cell line in which we did not observe synergy, we did not observe a substantial loss of active ERK in the combination-treated samples compared with RMC-7977 (Supplementary Fig. S3D). RMC-7977 caused a reduction in active Akt (pAkt) that was potentiated by combinations with erlotinib. However, as there was no synergy in this cell line, the MOA for synergistic growth suppression with RMC-7977 and erlotinib is largely independent of the PI3K pathway. Taken together, we speculate that patients with KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC may be more susceptible to RAS inhibitor + erlotinib combinations, due to EGFR inhibition preventing SOS1-mediated compensatory reactivation of WT RAS molecules necessary for activating the ERK MAPK pathway.

In addition to the KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cell lines, three of the nine KRASG12X-mutant PDAC cell lines we assessed exhibited a strong synergistic proliferative defect from erlotinib and RMC-7977 cotreatment. To determine whether we could establish a comutation profile or a subtyping signature that correlated with synergy, we evaluated genomic mutation status and performed bulk RNA-seq on all 12 cell lines, evaluating basal–classical signatures using both the Moffitt signatures and PurIST (Supplementary Table S6; refs. 36, 37). There was no correlation with subtyping signatures or comutation profiles while acknowledging the enrichment bias toward a basal phenotype in cell culture (54). We then performed gene set enrichment analyses using the Hallmark 50 gene set (55), and we could not identify any significantly dysregulated pathways (Supplementary Fig. S3E).

However, from our bulk RNA-seq analysis, we observed that EGFR expression levels were higher at baseline among the KRASG12X-mutant cell lines in which we observed antiproliferative synergy compared with those in which we did not (Fig. 4C; Supplementary Fig. S3F). We confirmed this trend at the EGFR protein and activity level (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. S3G). The combined treatment of RMC-7977 and erlotinib reduced active ERK in these cell lines more effectively compared with either inhibitor alone (Fig. 4E). Taken together, we conclude that the KRASG12X-mutant PDAC cell lines that have elevated EGFR expression/activity exhibit a strongly synergistic antiproliferative response to the combination of RMC-7977 and erlotinib.

To determine whether our findings could be recapitulated in patient-derived organoids in a defined medium with known concentrations of growth factors, we treated KRASG12D-mutant PDM-36 organoids with RMC-7977 and observed a dose-dependent proliferative defect (Supplementary Fig. S4A and S4B). Further, when we combined RMC-7977 with erlotinib, we observed synergistic growth suppression (Supplementary Fig. S4C).

Next, we cultured one KRASG12D-mutant cell line and two KRASQ61H cell lines in serum-depleted conditions (0.5% FBS) and assessed synergistic growth suppression (Supplementary Fig. S4D). Although we still observed synergistic growth suppression in all cell lines, the synergy was blunted in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC cells. This is consistent with our hypothesis that SOS1 reactivation of WT RAS alleles is dependent on EGFR stimulation in a KRASQ61H-mutant context.

Finally, to see if we could extend our findings to other EGFR-targeting agents with a distinct MOA, we substituted the EGFR-targeting monoclonal antibody cetuximab in place of erlotinib in AsPC-1 (KRASG12D) and T3M4 (KRASQ61H) cells and performed combination proliferation assays (Supplementary Fig. S4E). We determined that AsPC-1 cells treated with RMC-7977 + cetuximab had comparable synergistic growth suppression, while T3M4 cells exhibited blunted synergy compared with RMC-7977 + erlotinib.

Next, we evaluated effector signaling to determine the mechanism of the blunted synergistic growth suppression in T3M4 cells (Supplementary Fig. S4F). RMC-7977 decreased both active ERK and active Akt in both cell lines. We found that in AsPC-1 cells, both active ERK and active Akt were further suppressed in the combinations. In T3M4 cells, active Akt was further suppressed with combined RMC-7977 and cetuximab treatment, but cetuximab was not as effective at preventing compensatory ERK rebound activity. Overall, we conclude that EGFR targeting agents with distinct MOAs synergize with RMC-7977, albeit with different effects on downstream signaling pathways.

### Validating CK2 as a novel KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 LOF screening hit

We also sought to identify unexplored combination approaches. CK2 is a holoenzyme of CK2α, CK2α’, and CK2β, encoded by genes CSNK2A1, CSNK2A2, and CK2B, respectively (56, 57). Loss of CSNK2A2 was in the top 5% of KRASi sensitizing genes. When considering the RMC-7977 screens in isolation, loss of CSNK2A2 and CSNK2B scored as sensitizing genes. CSNK2A1 is associated with poor survival in a KRAS-independent manner (P = 8 × 10−4; ref. 58). CK2 (formerly casein kinase II) is a pleiotropic, ubiquitously expressed, constitutively active serine/threonine kinase with ∼500 kinase substrates.

SGC-CK2-1 is a selective tool compound CK2i (59), and another CK2i, silmitasertib (CX-4945), has been granted orphan drug status by the FDA (56). To determine whether either of these inhibitors synergized with KRASi to reduce proliferation in PDAC cell lines, we first combined MRTX1133 with SGC-CK2-1 in a panel of KRASG12D-mutant PDAC cell lines (Fig. 5A). SGC-CK2-1 alone caused a proliferative defect and mild-to-strong synergistic growth inhibition. We then extended this to a larger panel of KRAS-mutant PDAC cell lines using RMC-7977 and observed universal single-agent proliferative defects due to SGC-CK2-1, as well as proliferative synergy with RMC-7977 in all cell lines assessed (Fig. 5B). We next used the clinical candidate silmitasertib in combination with MRTX1133 and RMC-7977 and observed comparable results (Fig. 5C).

To interrogate the mechanism of synergy, we evaluated KRASi-sensitizing hits from our screening data that were CK2 substrates. Of the several CK2 substrates we identified, we initially focused on MYC for mechanistic follow-up, as CK2 has been reported to phosphorylate MYC at S347/S348, protecting MYC from proteasomal degradation (60–62). As there are currently no approved inhibitors of MYC (63), we posited that CK2 inhibition may be an indirect therapeutic approach to target MYC.

First, we utilized mass spectrometry to validate that MYC was phosphorylated by CK2 in an in vitro kinase assay. We determined that MYC was phosphorylated at both S347 and S348 but not dually phosphorylated on the same peptide (Supplementary Fig. S5A–S5H). We found that the addition of silmitasertib to the kinase assay substantially decreased CK2-dependent phosphorylation, as indicated by mass spectrometry, validating the on-target activity of the CK2i. To determine the impact of CK2 phosphorylation on MYC stability, we treated Pa14C cells with silmitasertib and cycloheximide to temporally monitor MYC protein half-life (Fig. 5D). In contrast to the literature (60, 61), we discovered that CK2 inhibition did not decrease MYC protein half-life in PDAC cells, suggesting that the combination of CK2i + KRASi synergizes due to MYC-independent mechanisms.

To further interrogate the mechanism underlying synergistic growth inhibition between CK2i and KRASi, we next pursued LEF1, another sensitizing hit in our screen. CK2 phosphorylates LEF1, which then complexes with β-catenin to enhance transcriptional activity (64). We previously validated β-catenin as a resistance driver to ERK inhibition (65). Using shRNAs targeting LEF1, we observed that knockdown of LEF1 with one of the two shRNAs sensitized HPAC cells to RMC-7977 (Supplementary Fig. S5I and S5J). Furthermore, LEF1 genetic suppression blunted synergistic growth inhibition between RMC-7977 and SGC-CK2-1 (Fig. 5E), suggesting that part of the mechanism underlying the synergistic growth inhibition with CK2 and KRASi may be attributed to LEF1.

As CK2 has been implicated in regulating autophagic flux and we have previously determined that autophagy inhibition synergistically induces apoptosis when combined with ERK inhibitors (66), we evaluated the role of CK2i on autophagic flux. However, we determined that CK2i potentiated, rather than prevented, RMC-7977-induced autophagic flux (Supplementary Fig. S5K). Thus, it is unlikely that CK2i-dependent autophagy is associated with the observed synergistic growth inhibition. Taken together, it is likely that there is a complex interplay of CK2 substrates, including LEF1, that leads to robust synergistic growth suppression when combined with KRASi in KRAS-mutant PDAC.

### Validating PI3K isoforms as a novel KRASi-anchored CRISPR-Cas9 LOF screening hit

We also identified loss of PIK3CG, encoding p110γ, as a sensitizing gene in our screens. We had previously determined that increased p110γ can act as a compensatory mechanism in KRASG12R-mutant PDAC to overcome the impaired binding of KRASG12R to the key RAS effector p110α (encoded by PIK3CA; ref. 41). Thus, we were surprised to see that PIK3CG also scored as a hit across different KRAS mutational subtypes despite their intact and functional binding to p110α. Notably, loss of PIK3CA also scored as a sensitizing gene in our screens. As both p110γ and p110α signal through Akt, we evaluated the impact of acute RMC-7977 treatment on active Akt in a panel of PDAC cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S6A). We observed that RMC-7977 caused a decrease in pAkt in five out of five cell lines, four of which rebounded by 72 hours.

Next, to determine the potential contribution of p110γ and/or p110α in modulating the response to RMC-7977, we overexpressed oncogenic forms of PIK3CG (L1018V) and PIK3CA (H1047R), utilizing oncogenic BRAF (V600E) as a control, in Pa14C cells and applied a dose response of RMC-7977 (Supplementary Fig. S6B). We determined that the expression of BRAFV600E most potently drove resistance to RMC-7977, followed by p110α H1047R and p110γ L1018V.

We next evaluated whether eganelisib (IPI-549), a p110γ-selective inhibitor (>150-fold more selective for p110γ than other PI3K isoforms) that has been granted fast-track designation by the FDA (67, 68), synergized with RMC-7977 to reduce proliferation. We treated nine cell lines with the combination of eganelisib and RMC-7977, and we observed mild to strong synergy across all nine of the KRAS-mutant PDAC cell lines at doses in which growth was inhibited (Supplementary Fig. S6C and S6E).

We next wanted to determine whether p110α inhibition exhibited similar synergistic effects by combining the PI3Kα-selective inhibitor alpelisib (>250-fold more selective for PI3Kα than other PI3K isoforms) with RMC-7977 in six PDAC cell lines (Supplementary Fig. S6D and S6F). Overall, we observed comparable results to eganelisib, with slightly stronger synergy with alpelisib combinations.

We did not observe synergistic growth suppression with either combination until alpelisib or eganelisib concentrations exceeded doses in which PI3K-isoform selectivity was lost, suggesting it is the concerted knockdown of multiple PI3K isoforms that causes synergistic growth suppression (67, 69). This is consistent with our previous observations in which we determined that combined inhibition of multiple PI3K isoforms is necessary to create a growth defect (70). It is possible that CRISPR technology, which completely ablates expression of the target gene, is potent enough for each individual isoform to selectively reduce proliferation when combined with KRASi. In contrast, PI3K isoform-selective inhibitors may not be able to achieve sufficient sensitivity before they lose PI3K-isoform selectivity. Taken together, we conclude that inhibition of p110γ and/or p110α in combination with RMC-7977 leads to synergistic growth reduction, potentially by converging on Akt signaling.

### RMC-7977–resistant PDAC cells undergo an EMT and are partially dependent on ERK MAPK signaling

To evaluate whether KRAS-mutant PDAC cell lines that did not exhibit synergy when cotreated with erlotinib and RMC-7977 would become dependent on EGFR in an acquired resistance setting, we generated a panel of RMC-7977–resistant cell lines. We began by treating PDAC cell lines that did not exhibit synergistic growth suppression with RMC-7977 + erlotinib with a GI50 of KRASi. When cells became confluent enough to passage, we increased the concentration by 50% or 100% with each passage, subjectively, for 10 weeks. We performed proliferation assays in the parental and resistant cells and determined that in all instances, the cell lines had GI50 >1,000-fold higher than the parental line (Fig. 6A; resistant cells designated with “R” at the end of the cell line names).

We assessed active EGFR, Akt, and ERK, as well as the nuclear ERK substrate MYC, longitudinally. After 10 weeks, we also assessed the activity levels of the cytoplasmic ERK substrate RSK (Fig. 6B). EGFR and Akt activity were inconsistent across the time points and cell lines. Thus, the cells were adapting during the 10-week period. Importantly, active ERK levels, MYC, and active RSK remained suppressed in all resistant cell lines. MYC and pRSK, ERK nuclear and cytoplasmic substrates, were also decreased.

We recently reported that in humans and animal models with PDAC, MYC amplification is a putative resistance driver to KRASi (10, 17). Thus, it was interesting that we did not observe MYC upregulation in our KRASi-resistant cells. It is possible that in heterogeneous in vivo tumors, there are cells preexisting with MYC amplification that get positively selected for upon chronic KRASi treatment that do not exist in cell culture. In support of this, we did see MYC upregulation in our surviving cells at the end of the pooled CRISPR screens, in which we genetically created a heterogeneous environment by removing genes that may regulate MYC levels. Further, as immunoblotting is a representation of a pooled population of cells, it is possible our analyses missed subclonal populations of cells with MYC amplification, and a technique like single-cell RNA-seq may be required to properly evaluate MYC amplification.

We also generated a panel of MRTX1133-resistant cell lines (designated “MR”), and by 4 weeks, pERK levels were similar in the parental and resistant cell lines in two out of three instances (Fig. 6C). MYC remained suppressed in the MRTX1133-resistant cell lines, so it is unclear whether ERK was actively modulating nuclear targets.

We next determined whether our RMC-7977–resistant cell lines had become dependent on EGFR by treating the parental and resistant lines with erlotinib (Fig. 6D). Across the panel of cell lines, both parental and resistant cell lines were relatively insensitive to erlotinib, suggesting RMC-7977–resistant cell lines are not more dependent on EGFR than their parental counterparts.

Next, we evaluated whether active RAS isoforms were elevated in the RMC-7977–resistant setting (Fig. 6E). Expectedly, in parental cell lines, KRASG12D was the dominantly GTP-loaded RAS isoform. However, in the RMC-7977–resistant setting, HRAS-GTP and NRAS-GTP were increased. KRAS-GTP was also substantially increased in Pa16C and PANC-1 cells, which are heterozygous for KRASG12D. Conversely, Pa14C cells did not show an increase in KRAS-GTP, likely because they exhibit loss of heterozygosity on the WT allele (24). However, as pERK was low in the resistant cell lines, RMC-7977 was likely still largely suppressing RAS-GTP.

We observed a gradual morphologic EMT in Pa14CR cells (Fig. 6F). Partial EMT has recently been characterized as a nongenomic resistance mechanism to MRTX1133 (10). To determine whether our RMC-7977–resistant cells had undergone a partial EMT, we evaluated EMT biomarkers (Fig. 6G). We determined that the Pa14CR cell line had undergone a full EMT, as indicated by a loss of E-cadherin, and increases in N-cadherin, vimentin, claudin-1, ZO-1, and EMT transcription factors. Pa16CR and PANC-1R cell lines exhibited a partial EMT phenotype.

We next assessed whether our Pa14CMR (MRTX1133-resistant) cell line had also undergone a full or partial EMT. We did not observe the same morphologic change, and analysis of EMT markers indicated that the cells had undergone a partial EMT (Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). We then assessed RAS-GTP levels in MRTX1133-resistant Pa14C cells, and we did not observe a substantial increase in any of the WT RAS-GTP levels (Supplementary Fig. S7C). We also observed a decrease in KRASG12D-GTP levels, consistent with the OFF-state inhibitor MRTX1133, which, like adagrasib, traps mutant KRAS in an inactive state (9).

We next sought to determine whether the EMT we observed in Pa14CR cells could drive resistance to RMC-7977. It has previously been determined that TGF-β treatment can drive resistance to KRAS genetic suppression by promoting EMT (23). Therefore, it was notable that Pa14CR cells underwent the most complete EMT, as they have a frameshift mutation in the SMAD4 gene, and a functional SMAD4 gene is required for TGF-β–driven EMT (24). To determine whether TGF-β could drive resistance to RMC-7977 in the SMAD4-mutated Pa14C cells, we treated Pa14C cells with TGF-β for 10 days and evaluated the response to RMC-7977 and EMT markers (Supplementary Fig. S7D and S7E). We observed that TGF-β treatment shifted the GI50 by more than 2-fold after treatment with RMC-7977. Interestingly, we did not observe as complete an EMT with TGF-β treatment as we observed in the RMC-7977–resistant Pa14CR cells. Thus, it is possible that some aspects of EMT associated with RMC-7977–resistant cells are TGF-β–independent. It remains unclear from our data the extent to which EMT is one of those mechanisms, and it is likely that there are EMT-independent mechanisms contributing to KRASi-driven resistance.

To determine whether the RMC-7977–resistant cell lines were dependent on ERK MAPK signaling for survival, we treated parental and resistant cell lines with the RAF inhibitor LY3009120 or the ERK inhibitor SCH772984 (Fig. 7A and B). Notably, although the resistant cell lines were >1,000-fold more resistant to RMC-7977, they retained sensitivity to both RAF and ERK inhibitors (2- to 4.3-fold resistant compared with parental cell lines). This was surprising given that active ERK was strongly suppressed at all time points.

## Discussion

A thorough understanding of genomic modulators of KRASi sensitivity is critical for determining therapeutic vulnerabilities and increasing the efficacy of KRASi in the clinic. In this study, we comprehensively profiled druggable genomic alterations that modulate KRASi sensitivity in a broad panel of PDAC cell lines. We validated both known and novel pharmacologically tractable hits from our screens. The combined dataset from our CRISPR screens also contains many robust unexplored hits for future studies. Additionally, we generated KRASi-resistant cell lines with acquired resistance. From these, we determined that PDAC cells with acquired resistance are still partially dependent on ERK MAPK signaling despite their decreased ERK signaling. We further determined that RMC-7977–resistant cell lines undergo a full or partial morphologic EMT, which we validated with biomarker analysis. We found that cells with acquired resistance to a KRASG12D inhibitor retained partial sensitivity to the pan-KRASi BI-2865 and the RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor RMC-7977. Finally, we discovered that RMC-7977–mediated acquired resistance was largely reversible after treatment removal. In summary, our findings provide several insights into resistance mechanisms to KRASi in PDAC with potential clinical implications.

We discovered that patients with KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC are pharmacologically and genetically less dependent on KRAS for survival. Mechanistically, we determined that this is at least partially due to biochemical differences between KRASQ61H and other KRAS mutations (39, 42, 43, 52, 53). We show that upon acute RMC-7977 treatment, SOS1 drives a compensatory increase in WT RAS and a rebound in active ERK in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC that does not occur as rapidly in KRASG12D-mutant PDAC. Combining an EGFRi with RMC-7977 prevents this active ERK rebound in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC, leading to synergistic growth suppression.

It has been well established that EGFR inhibition or SOS1 inhibition synergizes with mutant-selective KRASi (12, 20, 21, 49, 50, 71–73), and EGFR alterations have been found in patients with PDAC who develop resistance to KRASG12C inhibitors (10). Here, we observed synergy with the RAS(ON) multiselective inhibitor RMC-7977, which inhibits the ON state of both mutant and WT RAS (16), and erlotinib selectively in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC. Our findings highlight the possibility that distinct KRAS mutation subtypes may differentially respond to particular combinations and that patients with KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC, which has a poor prognosis, may be especially susceptible to KRASi + EGFRi combinations.

It was recently described that RMC-7977 synergizes with the EGFR monoclonal antibody cetuximab in G12, but not Q61 across a panel of RAS-mutant cancer cell lines (74). These findings were broad in scope, encompassing multiple cancer types (melanoma, pancreatic, and colon cancer), multiple RAS isoforms (KRAS and NRAS), and multiple G12X and Q61X mutations. In contrast, we focused on one tissue type (pancreas), one RAS isoform (KRAS), and one Q61 mutation (Q61H). Despite the narrower focus, our studies have many similarities. When comparing Hs766T cells and AsPC-1 cell lines, the common PDAC cell lines between our articles, our results are similar. Furthermore, we both identified PI3K isoforms in modulating sensitivity to RMC-7977, as we validated both PIK3CA and PIK3CG from our CRISPR screening data. However, we do observe differences from the prior work. By narrowing our focus to PDAC, KRAS, and Q61H, we identified subtype-specific differences in KRASQ61H-mutant PDAC that may or may not be extendable to other tissue types and RAS isoforms.

We also validated emerging therapeutic vulnerabilities like the pleiotropic kinase CK2. We observed synergy between CK2i and KRASi in all cell lines evaluated. Although we confirmed CK2 phosphorylates MYC at the regulatory sites S347 and/or S348, we found CK2i did not decrease MYC protein half-life, as seen in other contexts (60, 61). We propose that CK2-dependent phosphorylation of LEF1 and subsequent activation of a β-catenin–driven transcriptional program may contribute to the synergistic growth suppression, but the mechanisms underlying the synergy are likely multifactorial.

We developed a panel of RMC-7977–resistant PDAC cell lines and determined that cells intrinsically resistant to erlotinib do not become sensitized to it upon developing acquired resistance to KRASi. We observed a substantial increase in GTP loading of KRAS, HRAS, and NRAS upon acquisition of resistance to RMC-7977. Nevertheless, as RMC-7977 binds to the GTP-bound state of RAS, active ERK was decreased compared with the parental line at all time points in all cell lines. This indicates that RMC-7977 is likely preventing most downstream activation of ERK MAPK signaling, despite the increased RAS-GTP levels. Thus, we suspect the altered GTP loading of the RAS isoforms may be sufficient to maintain active ERK above a critical threshold, allowing cells to survive and slowly proliferate, facilitating alternative ERK-independent escape mechanisms, potentially like the full and partial EMT we observed. This is supported by our data indicating that the RMC-7977–resistant cell lines are partially sensitive to RAF inhibitors and ERK inhibitors, indicating residual dependence on ERK MAPK signaling.

We discovered that the RMC-7977-resistant cells proliferate more slowly than their parental counterparts, and upon RMC-7977 removal for 30 days, the cells resume their proliferative capacity. After this 30-day treatment removal, the cells are responsive to RMC-7977. We found that MRTX1133-resistant PDAC cell lines are partially sensitive to BI-2865 and RMC-7977, suggesting that patients resistant to a mutant-selective inhibitor might still respond to a pan-KRAS or multiselective RAS inhibitor. Overall, our data support that intrinsic and acquired resistance to KRASi may vary by KRAS mutational subtype and inhibitor MOA. In summary, we have validated both known KRASi resistance mechanisms and identified previously undescribed KRASi resistance mechanisms, some of which may be rapidly translatable.
